title: What Makes a House a House — Then Back to Sukkah
subtitle: Finishing the 4-amos digression, and the point it was all for: a sukkah, being temporary, doesn't need nearly as much.
sources: Gemara text: Sefaria (William Davidson Edition). Structure and quiz questions 3-6 cross-checked against the Dafyomi Advancement Forum (dafyomi.co.il) quiz for Sukkah 3. The closing point continues onto 4a.
before: 3a opened a tangent: what makes a structure legally count as a "house"? This amud finishes that list, then delivers the actual point of the detour — even though a permanent house needs 4×4 amos to count as a dwelling, a sukkah is temporary, so the Rabbis allow it to be smaller.

The amud closes with the tangent's own engine room: courtyard-division mechanics between neighbors with different numbers of entrances. It ends on a fresh question for the main sukkah topic, picked up on 4a — does piling cushions and blankets on the floor count as lowering an over-height sukkah?

flowCaption: The tangent resolves back into the sukkah theme, then its own mechanics run to the end of the amud.

opinions.claim: Even they agree a house needs 4×4 amos to count as a dwelling — but that's specific to a permanent residence. A sukkah, being a temporary dwelling, doesn't need nearly that much.
opinions.basis: <he>לְעִנְיַן סוּכָּה דְּדִירַת עֲרַאי הִיא, אֲבָל לְגַבֵּי בַּיִת דְּדִירַת קֶבַע הוּא</he> — the tangent's actual payoff.

opinions.claim: A courtyard is divided among its residents in proportion to how many entrances each of them has.
Each entrance first gets a flat 4 amos off the top; only what's left over is split evenly among the residents.
opinions.basis: A different mechanism for the same courtyard-division question.

script.speaker: List continues
script.quote: וְאֵין עוֹשִׂין אוֹתוֹ עִיבּוּר בֵּין שְׁתֵּי עֲיָירוֹת, וְאֵין הָאַחִין וְהַשּׁוּתָּפִין חוֹלְקִין בּוֹ.
script.gloss: A sub-4-amos house also can't count toward joining two cities for Shabbat-boundary purposes, and brothers or partners can't force its division — it's too small to divide.

script.speaker: Gemara asks
script.gloss: Is this beraita's author Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi alone (who elsewhere requires 4 amos even for a sukkah), and not the Rabbis?

script.speaker: Resolution
script.quote: לְעִנְיַן סוּכָּה — דְּדִירַת עֲרַאי הִיא ... אֲבָל לְגַבַּי בַּיִת — דְּדִירַת קֶבַע הוּא, אֲפִילּוּ רַבָּנַן מוֹדוּ.
script.gloss: Even the Rabbis could hold this: they only require less than 4 amos for a sukkah, which is a temporary dwelling. For a house, a permanent dwelling, even the Rabbis agree it needs a full 4×4 amos to count as a livable house at all.

script.speaker: Reason-by-reason
script.gloss: The Gemara works through the list: mezuzah, parapet, tzaraat-impurity, and the walled-city sale rules all depend on Torah verses that specifically say "house" — so they don't apply to a structure too small to count as one.

script.speaker: Eiruv vs. shittuf
script.gloss: A sub-4-amos house can't hold the food for eiruvei chatzeirot (joining a courtyard's households) — it isn't fit for residence. But it can hold the food for shittufei mevoyos (merging an alleyway's courtyards), since for that purpose it's no worse than an ordinary open courtyard.

script.speaker: On dividing it
script.gloss: Brothers or partners can't force a sub-4-amos house to be divided the way a courtyard is divided — that whole division framework simply doesn't apply to something this small.

script.speaker: Courtyard mechanics
script.gloss: How is a shared courtyard actually divided among residents? Rav Huna: proportionally, by how many entrances each resident has onto it. Rav Chisda: each entrance first gets a flat 4 amos, and only the remaining space is split evenly.

script.speaker: Looking ahead
script.gloss: The Gemara returns to the sukkah's own height law: if a sukkah is more than 20 amos high and someone piles cushions and blankets on the floor to bring it under the line, that reduction doesn't count — continued on 4a.
